::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The decision this serves
Is this target reachable by this modality? Answering it needs one physical fact
— where the protein sits — and one chemical one: what it takes to bind it.
Get either wrong and years of work go into a molecule that can never arrive.
:::

## 1. The cell, in the parts that matter

A cell is a bag of water, wrapped in a greasy membrane, full of machines made of
protein.

**The membrane** is two layers of fat molecules arranged tail-to-tail, about
5 nanometres thick. Its interior is oily. This one fact explains most of
pharmacokinetics: to cross it unaided, a molecule must be at least somewhat
comfortable in oil. Water-loving molecules and charged ions cannot pass, which is
why the body needs dedicated protein channels and transporters to move them —
and why those transporters keep reappearing in later lessons as the thing that
moves your drug, or refuses to.

**The interior** is crowded, aqueous and busy. Roughly one-fifth to one-third of
it by volume is protein.

**Compartments inside** matter for drugs. The nucleus holds DNA — the target of
some anticancer agents. Lysosomes are acidic pockets in which basic drugs
accumulate by the trapping mechanism `P-08` covers. Mitochondria generate energy
and are a common site of toxicity.

## 2. Proteins are shapes, and the shape is the function

A protein is a chain of amino acids that folds into a specific three-dimensional
shape. That shape is everything: it creates pockets and surfaces, and those
pockets are where drugs bind.

Four families cover most of what medicine does:

- **Receptors** receive signals. Something binds on the outside; the protein
  changes shape; something happens inside. Most hormones and neurotransmitters
  work this way, and so do a large share of drugs.
- **Enzymes** catalyse reactions — building, breaking, modifying molecules.
  Inhibiting an enzyme is the mechanism behind statins, ACE inhibitors and most
  antivirals.
- **Transporters** move things across membranes, often against a gradient and at
  metabolic cost.
- **Ion channels** are gated pores. Opening or closing them changes a cell's
  electrical state, which is how local anaesthetics and many cardiac drugs work.

`P-03` takes each in turn. What matters here is that **all four are proteins with
pockets**, and a drug works by occupying a pocket.

## 3. Binding is reversible sticking, not gluing

This is the concept everything quantitative rests on, and the everyday intuition
is misleading.

A drug molecule and its target are both jostling in water at body temperature.
When they meet in the right orientation, weak forces hold them together:
electrostatic attraction, hydrogen bonds, and — usually the largest contributor —
the hydrophobic effect, in which oily surfaces stick together mostly because
water prefers to be elsewhere. None of these is a chemical bond. Any one is
easily broken by thermal jostling; several acting together are not.

So binding is **reversible** and **dynamic**:

$$\text{Drug} + \text{Target} \rightleftharpoons \text{Drug–Target complex}$$

At any instant some fraction of targets is occupied. Individual molecules are
constantly arriving and leaving. Nothing is permanent, and the population
statistic — *what fraction is occupied right now* — is what matters, not the fate
of any one molecule.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**A single drug molecule does nothing measurable.** A therapeutic dose delivers
something on the order of 10²⁰ molecules. Pharmacology is a statistical science
about enormous populations of molecules and targets, which is exactly why
continuous mathematics describes it so well. When `P-04` writes occupancy as a
smooth curve, that smoothness is real, not an approximation.
:::

### Two exceptions worth knowing

**Covalent drugs** form a true chemical bond and do not come off. Aspirin works
this way, as do several modern kinase inhibitors. For these, the effect outlasts
the drug's presence entirely: the molecule is long cleared while its targets stay
disabled until the cell makes new ones. That decoupling breaks the usual
concentration–effect link, and needs a model built around protein turnover rather
than plasma concentration.

**Very slow dissociation** produces something similar without a covalent bond.
If a drug takes hours to let go, its effect tracks how long it stays bound rather
than what the plasma concentration is doing. This is *residence time*, and it is
why two drugs with identical affinity can behave completely differently in
patients — a point `P-04` makes with numbers.

## 4. Selectivity, and why side effects are usually on-target

The human body makes around twenty thousand different proteins, and many are
structural cousins. A pocket that fits your drug may be nearly duplicated on a
protein doing something entirely different somewhere else.

**Selectivity** is how much more tightly a drug binds its intended target than
the alternatives. It is a ratio, never a yes or no — and because occupancy
depends on concentration, selectivity is a *dose-dependent property*. A drug that
is beautifully selective at a low dose can lose that selectivity at a higher one,
as concentrations climb high enough to occupy the off-targets too.

This is the quantitative core of the therapeutic window, and it reframes side
effects usefully:

- **On-target, wrong place.** The drug hits exactly the protein it was designed
  for, in tissue where you did not want that. Most predictable adverse effects
  are this.
- **Off-target.** The drug hits a different protein. Often a surprise, and often
  what a safety pharmacology screen is looking for.
- **On-target, too much.** An exaggerated version of the intended effect —
  a blood-pressure drug that lowers it too far.

Only the second is a selectivity failure in the narrow sense. The others are
dose and distribution problems, which is to say: modelling problems.

## 5. What this means for models

Three things you can carry into every later strand.

**Effect follows occupancy, not dose.** Dose sets concentration; concentration
sets occupancy; occupancy sets effect. Each arrow is a separate process with its
own timing, and each can break independently. A drug can fail because it never
reached adequate concentration, or reached it and did not bind, or bound and the
biology compensated.

**Only free drug binds.** Drug stuck to plasma proteins is not available. When a
clinical concentration is compared against an *in vitro* potency, the comparison
is only meaningful on free drug — the trap `S0-02` catches with `CASE-SM`, where
using total instead of free concentration flips the conclusion.

**Timescales rarely match.** Binding equilibrates in seconds. Plasma
concentrations change over hours. Downstream biology can take days. When
processes are separated by orders of magnitude you can often treat the fast one
as instantaneous — an approximation that makes most PK/PD models tractable, and
that fails loudly when the separation is not there.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Failure mode — treating potency as a property of the drug alone
A compound has an IC₅₀ of 10 nM in one assay and 300 nM in another, and the team
concludes one measurement was wrong.

Both may be right. A competition assay's IC₅₀ depends on how much competing
substrate or radioligand is present, because the drug has to out-compete it. Add
more competitor and the same drug looks weaker. The Cheng–Prusoff relationship in
`P-04` converts an IC₅₀ into a K~i~, which *is* a property of the drug–target
pair — and it needs the assay conditions to do so.

The general lesson: **an IC₅₀ without its assay conditions is not a number you
can use.** Modellers inherit these values from *in vitro* colleagues constantly.
Ask what was in the well.
:::

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Why can an antibody not hit an intracellular target?
It cannot cross the cell membrane. The membrane's oily interior admits small,
reasonably lipophilic molecules; an antibody is a large, water-loving protein
with no route in. Antibodies work on things outside cells — circulating proteins,
and the outward-facing parts of membrane proteins. This is why target location
constrains modality before any chemistry begins, and why "is the target
extracellular?" is one of the first questions asked about a new programme.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Two drugs have identical K~d~. Can they still behave differently in patients?
Yes, for at least three reasons. **Residence time**: K~d~ is a ratio of on- and
off-rates, so two drugs can share it while one dissociates in seconds and the
other in hours — and the slow one's effect persists after plasma concentrations
fall. **Free fraction**: if one is 99% protein-bound and the other 50%, the same
total concentration delivers very different free concentrations. **Access**: if
the target is intracellular or behind the blood–brain barrier, the drug that gets
there wins regardless of affinity. Affinity is one number in a chain of several.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Why is selectivity dose-dependent?
Because occupancy depends on concentration, and every target has its own
concentration–occupancy curve. Suppose the intended target has K~d~ 10 nM and an
off-target 1 µM — a hundredfold selectivity. At 10 nM free drug you occupy half
the intended target and about 1% of the off-target. At 1 µM you occupy nearly all
of the intended target and half the off-target. Nothing about the molecule
changed; the dose did. This is why a safety margin is expressed as a ratio of
*exposures*, not as a property of the compound.
:::

  `S1` builds target-mediated disposition on exactly this picture.
- **Reference:** Kenakin T, *Receptor theory*
  ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471141755.ph0102s41)) for the quantitative
  treatment of everything in this lesson. Textbooks: Alberts, *Molecular Biology
  of the Cell*, on membranes and protein function — dense but the standard; Rang
  & Dale for the pharmacology-first version.

*Seen in the wild:* a programme once spent eighteen months optimising affinity
from 5 nM to 0.5 nM. Clinical effect did not improve, because at the doses given
the target was already fully occupied. Affinity beyond what saturates the target
buys nothing — a fact a simple occupancy calculation would have shown before the
chemistry started. `P-04` is that calculation.
